netlicensing-mcp get_product called with path-traversal product_number (../token) AIExploitation High
Hunts MCP/application-log evidence of the netlicensing_get_product tool being invoked with a product_number containing path-traversal sequences (../, %2e%2e, %2f, %5c). This is the raw attacker input for GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8, captured before httpx normalizes /product/../token into /token. Rationale: Uses the exact MCP tool name (netlicensing_get_product) plus the article's documented traversal payloads (../token and the encoded variants %2e%2e/%2f/%5c the remediation adds regression tests for). A Product-fetch tool receiving path separators in its identifier argument has no legitimate use. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: the payload is an in-process MCP tool argument, not a Windows process command line or AWS API call. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/netlicensing-mcp/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8/ • https://netlicensing.io/wiki/restful-api • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • DAST/WAF vulnerability scanner probing the MCP server with traversal fuzz strings

  • Internal red-team validation of the GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 patch
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("regression-test", "pytest", "VULN-001", "scanner"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full log line — confirm the tool is netlicensing_get_product and the product_number literally contains ../ , %2e%2e, %2f or %5c. Identify the MCP client identity / API key that made the call. 2) CONTAIN: If product is < 0.1.8, treat as confirmed exploit — rotate the NetLicensing API key the MCP server holds, and any APIKEY tokens (especially ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN) that could have been disclosed; upgrade to >=0.1.8. 3) HUNT: Search the same source for other tool calls from this client and for get_product responses containing tokenType/APIKEY (UC3) to confirm whether a key was actually returned.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "netlicensing_get_product"
| where SyslogMessage contains "../" or SyslogMessage contains "..\\" or SyslogMessage contains "%2e%2e" or SyslogMessage contains "%2f" or SyslogMessage contains "%5c"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog netlicensing_get_product AND ("../" OR "%2e%2e" OR "%2f" OR "%5c")
APPLICATION

| table _time host source _raw
| sort - _time
NetLicensing REST request URL containing both /product/ and traversal-to-token (wire signature) AIExploitation High
Hunts forward-proxy / SWG logs for a single request to go.netlicensing.io (or backup netlicensing.labs64.com) whose URL contains the /product/ segment together with /token or an encoded traversal sequence — the on-the-wire artefact when the percent-encoded GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 payload survives httpx normalization. Legitimate traffic hits /product OR /token, never both in one URL. Rationale: Anchors on the confirmed REST base host go.netlicensing.io (+backup netlicensing.labs64.com) and the structural impossibility of a legitimate URL containing both /product/ and a token/traversal segment. Targets the encoded variants (%2e%2e/%2f/%5c) that survive WHATWG normalization to the wire. Datadog empty: no web-proxy source in this tenant's source list; Defender/Falcon empty: no HTTP path visibility inside HTTPS to a SaaS endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/netlicensing-mcp/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8/ • https://netlicensing.io/wiki/restful-api

netlicensing-mcp get_product response leaking APIKEY/token fields (redaction bypass) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts MCP/application logs for a netlicensing_get_product (Product-typed) tool call whose output contains token-specific fields — tokenType APIKEY, ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN, or a console_url under /#/tokens/. Per GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 these are exactly the fields redact_token_read() would mask; a Product tool returning them is direct evidence the traversal reached /token and leaked a plaintext key. Rationale: Pairs the Product tool name with the exact token-leak markers from the advisory's PoC output (tokenType=APIKEY, role ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN, console_url https://ui.netlicensing.io/#/tokens/<key>). The legitimate token tools (get_token/list_tokens) may emit these too, but a PRODUCT tool emitting them is unambiguous bypass evidence. Hunting tier because it depends on the deployment logging tool responses. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: app-layer response content unavailable to those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/netlicensing-mcp/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8
ATT&CKT1212 T1552
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Verbose debug logging that echoes a legitimate get_token response near a get_product log line (correlation artefact)
  • Replay of the published PoC output in a test/log-sample dataset
  • A custom downstream tool that legitimately enriches product data with token metadata (rare; should be validated)
  • Log aggregation that interleaves get_product and get_token messages making string co-occurrence appear in one record
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the record is a get_product RESPONSE (not a get_token call) carrying a real (unmasked) APIKEY number/console_url. Note the MCP client identity and the leaked token's role. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately revoke/rotate the disclosed APIKEY token — if ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN, treat the entire NetLicensing account as compromised (full read/write/delete) and rotate the account owner credential; upgrade to >=0.1.8. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all get_product calls from this client (UC1) to scope which keys were exfiltrated, and review NetLicensing audit/console activity for use of the leaked admin token.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "netlicensing_get_product"
| where SyslogMessage has "ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN" or (SyslogMessage has "tokenType" and SyslogMessage has "APIKEY") or SyslogMessage contains "/#/tokens/"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog netlicensing_get_product AND ("ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN" OR "tokenType" OR "/#/tokens/")
APPLICATION
index=* "netlicensing_get_product" ("ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN" OR "tokenType" OR "/#/tokens/")
| table _time host source _raw
| sort - _time
First-seen access to NetLicensing /token REST endpoint from MCP egress source AIActions on Objectives Medium
Behavioral baseline over proxy logs: flags a source host issuing GET /core/v2/rest/token to go.netlicensing.io when that source has no prior history of token-endpoint access in the baseline window. This covers the GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 case where the literal ../token payload is normalized by httpx to a bare /token request that carries no traversal artefact on the wire. Rationale: Catches the literal ../token variant that UC2 misses (httpx collapses /product/../token to a bare /token GET). Because the dedicated token tools also legitimately hit /token, this relies on a 14-day per-source baseline so only newly-token-active sources surface — Medium confidence by design. Anchored on the confirmed REST path /core/v2/rest/token. Datadog empty (no proxy source in tenant list); Defender/Falcon empty (no HTTPS path visibility). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/netlicensing-mcp/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8/ • https://netlicensing.io/wiki/restful-api

Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("")  // populate with confirmed-benign MCP/token-tool egress IPs after first triage to suppress benign new-adopter sources
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the new source's /token access correlates with a get_product call in MCP/app logs (UC1/UC3). If the source is the MCP server host and no legitimate token tool was invoked, treat as the normalized traversal. 2) CONTAIN: Rotate any APIKEY tokens the source could have read; confirm package >=0.1.8. 3) HUNT: Add confirmed-benign token-using sources to an allowlist, then widen the window to look for repeated first-seen token access across other hosts.

Vulnerable googleapis/mcp-toolbox (< 1.4.0) — CVE-2026-11718 opaque-token auth bypass present AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces any managed host whose vulnerability feed reports CVE-2026-11717 / CVE-2026-11718 against the googleapis/mcp-toolbox Go package. This hunts the specific auth-bypass advisory (validateOpaqueToken accepting introspection responses that omit the mandatory RFC 7662 "active" field), not a generic missing-patch query — it anchors on the exact CVE IDs and the mcp-toolbox software name. Rationale: Anchors on the article's two concrete identifiers (CVE-2026-11717/11718) and the affected package name github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox; deterministic CVE-feed match, so FP is limited to stale-inventory rather than behavioural noise. Cross-checked the GHSA against CyberPress, CyberSecurityNews and the upstream GitHub issue #3076 which confirm fix version 1.4.0 and CVSS 4.0 9.3. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcpr-6g7x-p44r • https://github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox/issues/3076 • https://cyberpress.org/mcp-toolbox-vulnerability-exposed/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/mcp-toolbox-vulnerability/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-11718
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already upgraded to 1.4.0+ but the TVM/scanner snapshot is stale and a re-scan is still pending
  • CVE feed maps the Go module under a SoftwareName that doesn't contain 'toolbox' (vendor naming drift), so a real device is missed rather than false-positive
  • Isolated dev/CI box intentionally pinned to an old version inside a non-routable network
  • Vendored / build-artifact copy of the module flagged as 'installed' though no toolbox service is actually listening
  • Container image scanned by the feed though the image is ephemeral and already destroyed
Suppression filter
| join kind=inner (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | where SoftwareName has_any ("mcp-toolbox","toolbox") | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId | extend CleanVer = trim_start(@"[vV]", SoftwareVersion) | where CleanVer matches regex @"^\d+(\.\d+)+" | where parse_version(CleanVer) < parse_version("1.4.0")) on DeviceId
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each dest/DeviceName, confirm a mcp-toolbox process is actually listening (default port 5000) and note whether it's internet-facing; pull SoftwareVersion to verify it is genuinely < 1.4.0 and not a stale record. 2) CONTAIN: Patch to >= 1.4.0 (the fixed release); if patching is delayed, restrict the toolbox's network exposure to trusted clients and verify the configured OAuth introspection endpoint is a trusted, RFC 7662-compliant server that always returns the 'active' field. 3) HUNT: Review toolbox/auth access logs for tool invocations that succeeded against an introspection response lacking 'active', and check for the sibling advisories on the same hosts (CVE-2026-9739 SSE DNS-rebinding, and the issuer-field bypass variant).

| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-11717", "CVE-2026-11718")
| where SoftwareVendor has "google" or SoftwareName has_any ("mcp-toolbox", "toolbox")
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId, CveId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Internet-facing host running vulnerable mcp-toolbox (< 1.4.0) — exposed auth-bypass surface AIExploitation Medium
Prioritises CVE-2026-11718 exposure by cross-referencing the mcp-toolbox software inventory (version < 1.4.0, the fixed release) against assets flagged internet-facing. Targets the externally reachable instances where an attacker-influenced or non-compliant introspection endpoint could trigger the validateOpaqueToken bypass — a different pivot (inventory + exposure join) than the raw CVE-feed match. Rationale: Uses the article's fixed-version boundary (1.4.0) for an explicit parse_version comparison and the package name, then joins DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing to rank externally exposed instances — the highest-risk targets for a remote token-validation bypass (T1190). Sentinel lacks the DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory table, so the Sentinel variant expresses the same intent via the CVE feed joined to internet-facing assets. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcpr-6g7x-p44r • https://cyberpress.org/mcp-toolbox-vulnerability-exposed/ • https://github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox/issues/3076
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SoftwareVersion carries a pre-release/build suffix (e.g. '1.4.0-rc1') that passes the regex but is functionally patched
  • IsInternetFacing flag is stale — host has since been moved behind a firewall or load balancer
  • mcp-toolbox present only as a transitive SDK/library, not the exposed listening server
  • Reverse proxy / WAF fronts the toolbox so the flagged host is exposed but the toolbox port is not actually reachable
  • Inventory shows old version string cached after an in-place binary swap to 1.4.0
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.4." and SoftwareVersion !startswith "v1.4."
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the toolbox listener is reachable from the public IP (probe the configured port, default 5000) and that SoftwareVersion is genuinely < 1.4.0; validate the OAuth introspection endpoint it trusts is RFC 7662-compliant and always emits 'active'. 2) CONTAIN: Take the external exposure offline or front it with auth-enforcing proxy; upgrade to >= 1.4.0. 3) HUNT: Pull the toolbox/auth logs for the exposure window and look for tool-invocation successes tied to introspection responses missing 'active', plus the related SSE DNS-rebinding (CVE-2026-9739) and issuer-omission bypass on the same internet-facing fleet.

| sort by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Kirby Panel install surface accessed on a live site (CVE-2026-54003) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts any HTTP request to the Kirby Panel installation routes (/panel/installation or /api/system/install) on a production site. An already-initialised Kirby install never legitimately serves these routes, so traffic here on a live site indicates external-initialization probing or exploitation of CVE-2026-54003 via the spoofable Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP headers. Rationale: Uses the exact Kirby install routes /panel/installation and /api/system/install named in the advisory and confirmed in Kirby docs; on a live site any non-404/403 hit is anomalous. Client-IP filtering is deliberately omitted because behind a reverse proxy the logged cIP is the proxy, not the attacker (the spoofed IP lives in the Forwarded/X-Real-IP header). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-whxw-24jc-cwmv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/getkirby/cms/CVE-2026-54003/ • https://github.com/getkirby/kirby/releases/tag/5.4.4
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internet background scanners probing common CMS/admin paths like /panel
  • Legitimate first-time deployment of a brand-new Kirby site within the maintenance window
  • Authorized vulnerability scanning or pentest engagement against the site
  • Synthetic uptime/availability monitors crawling Panel routes
  • Staging/dev Kirby instance shipping access logs into the same workspace
Suppression filter
| where toint(scStatus) !in (404, 403)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull all install-route hits; check the response code and whether this host is a brand-new deploy (no admin yet) versus an established site. Cross-reference proxy logs for the Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP header and the true client IP. 2) Contain: If the site was already live, treat as compromise — set 'api'=>false or take Panel offline, and update Kirby to 4.9.4/5.4.4. 3) Hunt: Pivot to UC 'admin account created' to see if a POST succeeded, then review Panel logins, new users, and uploaded templates/plugins for webshells.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "/panel/installation" or csUriStem has "/api/system/install"
| where toint(scStatus) !in (404, 403)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kirby remote first-admin creation via unauthenticated install POST (CVE-2026-54003) AIInstallation High
Alerts on a successful POST to the Kirby install API (/api/system/install or /panel/installation) returning a 2xx status. On a publicly reachable Kirby site this means the first admin account was created without authentication by abusing the Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP isLocal bypass — the actual exploitation and persistence step of CVE-2026-54003. Rationale: Keys on the exact install API route plus method=POST and a 2xx response — a combination that on an already-deployed Kirby site means an admin was actually created without auth, which is the precise impact the advisory describes. Status filter separates successful exploitation from harmless scanner probes. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-whxw-24jc-cwmv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/getkirby/cms/CVE-2026-54003/ • https://github.com/getkirby/kirby/releases/tag/5.4.4
ATT&CKT1190 T1136
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentional first-time install by an admin with panel.install enabled during a deploy window
  • DevOps automation that provisions the first admin via the install endpoint
  • Fresh staging/dev deploy that legitimately has no users yet
  • A redeploy that wiped the accounts/ directory and is being re-initialised on purpose
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm scStatus 2xx on the POST and verify the site was already live (had an admin) rather than a planned new deploy; capture cIP and the true client IP from proxy Forwarded/X-Real-IP headers. 2) Contain: Immediately delete the attacker-created admin account, invalidate all Panel sessions, set 'api'=>false or take the Panel offline, and upgrade to Kirby 4.9.4/5.4.4. 3) Hunt: Review all Panel logins and actions from the new account, content/blueprint/template changes, additional user creations, and any uploaded PHP for webshells; pivot on the source IP across other sites.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "/api/system/install" or csUriStem has "/panel/installation"
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where toint(scStatus) in (200, 201)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Hacker News
2026-06-18 9 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft has disclosed details of a Windows-based cryptocurrency clipper campaign codenamed CryptoBandits that has targeted users since February 2026 with clipboard-intercepting malware with self-spreading capabilities and using the Tor anonymity network to hide communication. "The clipper in this campaign relies on Windows Script Host and ActiveX-driven logic to launch a bundled Tor proxy and

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] USB LNK worm cloning documents into shortcuts - CryptoBandits propagation
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Windows Script Host (wscript/cscript) spawning renamed Tor proxy, curl or shell - CryptoBandits clipper · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Scheduled task persistence created by Windows Script Host - CryptoBandits worm/clipper · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Renamed portable Tor client (ugate.exe / Tor metadata masquerade) - CryptoBandits SOCKS5 backdoor · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PowerShell screen capture staged for Tor exfiltration - CryptoBandits clipper · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Windows Script Host (wscript/cscript) spawning renamed Tor proxy, curl or shell - CryptoBandits clipper AIExploitation High
Hunts the CryptoBandits clipper's core execution behaviour: a WScript/CScript host launching the bundled Tor client (ugate.exe), curl, cmd or PowerShell. Microsoft explicitly recommends behavioural detection of script engines spawning these binaries for this campaign. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated execution chain (WScript/ActiveX launching a bundled Tor proxy + curl/cmd/PowerShell) and the corroborated Tor binary name ugate.exe; the ProcessVersionInfoProductName has 'Tor' clause catches the binary even if renamed away from ugate.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://www.securityweek.com/cryptobandits-malware-doubles-as-a-backdoor-abuses-tor/ • https://cyberpress.org/tor-proxy-malware-control/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business VBScript/JScript installers that shell out to cmd.exe for setup tasks
  • Admin logon scripts (wscript) that call curl.exe to fetch config or PowerShell for inventory
  • Software deployment frameworks (SCCM/Intune) that wrap script-host bootstrappers around rundll32
  • Privileged orchestration tooling running scheduled VBScripts that spawn powershell.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Microsoft\", @"\CCM\", @"\Intune") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and the wscript/cscript ParentCmd; confirm the script path and whether the child is ugate.exe / a binary carrying Tor version metadata. Check the script's origin folder (removable drive or %TEMP%/%APPDATA%). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the wscript/cscript and child process tree, and block the script + ugate.exe hashes. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for localhost:9050 connections, schtasks /create by script host, mass .lnk creation on drives, and PowerShell screen-capture - the other CryptoBandits stages.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("ugate.exe","tor.exe","curl.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Tor"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildProduct = ProcessVersionInfoProductName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\ugate.exe", @"\tor.exe", @"\curl.exe", @"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\mshta.exe", @"\rundll32.exe", @"\regsvr32.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Windows Script Host Spawning Tor Proxy, curl or Shell (CryptoBandits Clipper)
id: 7f1c9a2e-3b54-4d77-9a1e-2c0f8b6d4a11
description: Detects wscript.exe or cscript.exe launching the bundled Tor client (ugate.exe), curl, cmd or PowerShell as seen in the CryptoBandits USB clipper campaign.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.005
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\ugate.exe'
      - '\tor.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe) @Image:(*\\ugate.exe OR *\\UGate.exe OR *\\tor.exe OR *\\Tor.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(ugate|tor|curl|cmd|powershell|pwsh|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("ugate.exe","tor.exe","curl.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where user!="*$"
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("ugate.exe","tor.exe","curl.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where user!="*$"
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Renamed portable Tor client (ugate.exe / Tor metadata masquerade) - CryptoBandits SOCKS5 backdoor AICommand & Control High
Identifies the CryptoBandits portable Tor client deployed as ugate.exe, or any binary carrying The Tor Project's PE version metadata while renamed away from tor.exe. This Tor instance opens a local SOCKS5 proxy on 127.0.0.1:9050 to reach the hidden-service C2. Rationale: Uses the corroborated renamed-Tor IOC ugate.exe plus a masquerade clause (Tor PE metadata on a non-tor.exe image) so the rule survives a rename; the SOCKS5-on-9050 behaviour described in the article is what this binary stands up. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/tor-proxy-malware-control/ • https://www.securityweek.com/cryptobandits-malware-doubles-as-a-backdoor-abuses-tor/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1036.005 T1564.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tor Browser Bundle installs where the user legitimately runs tor.exe (excluded), but a portable copy renamed by a power user could trip the metadata clause
  • Privacy/anonymity research tooling that bundles a renamed Tor binary
  • Pentest/red-team toolkits shipping Tor under a non-standard name during sanctioned engagements
  • Security products that embed a Tor stub with their own product metadata
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","explorer.exe","cmd.exe") or FileName =~ "ugate.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the image's PE metadata (CompanyName 'The Tor Project', OriginalFileName tor.exe) versus its on-disk name; capture SHA256 and the launching parent (expect wscript/cscript). 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate ugate.exe, block the hash, and capture netstat for a 127.0.0.1:9050 listener. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent script, scheduled tasks created by script host, and clipboard/screenshot activity to scope full CryptoBandits infection.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "ugate.exe"
    or ((ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Tor" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "tor.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Tor") and FileName !in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          OriginalFileName = ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName,
          Company = ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\ugate.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Renamed Portable Tor Client - CryptoBandits ugate.exe SOCKS5 Backdoor
id: 2a9d6c41-8e07-4b3a-bb22-91f5e3d7c508
description: Detects the CryptoBandits Tor client deployed as ugate.exe, or any image carrying Tor original-filename metadata while renamed away from tor.exe.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Scheduled task persistence created by Windows Script Host - CryptoBandits worm/clipper AIInstallation High
Detects the CryptoBandits worm registering scheduled-task persistence for both the worm and the clipper module by having wscript.exe/cscript.exe invoke schtasks.exe /create. Script-host-created scheduled tasks are rare in benign environments. Rationale: Article states the worm deploys scheduled tasks for both the worm and the stealer; pairing schtasks /create with a script-host parent is high-fidelity because benign scheduled tasks are almost never created by wscript/cscript interactively. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://cyberinsider.com/microsoft-warns-of-usb-worm-like-malware-using-tor-for-stealth/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy application setup VBScripts that register a maintenance scheduled task on first run
  • Admin/MDM logon scripts that create user-level scheduled tasks via schtasks
  • Software updaters bootstrapped from a .vbs wrapper that self-schedule recurring checks
  • Helpdesk remediation scripts run interactively that create a one-off cleanup task
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Microsoft\", "updater") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full schtasks /create command line - capture /tn task name, /tr action (expect it to point at wscript running the worm/clipper script or ugate.exe), and the parent script path. 2) Contain: delete the malicious task (schtasks /delete /tn <name>), isolate the host, and kill the script-host tree. 3) Hunt: enumerate all scheduled tasks on the host and across the fleet whose action references wscript/cscript or ugate.exe; check for the paired worm + clipper tasks the campaign installs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          TaskCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scheduled Task Created by Windows Script Host (CryptoBandits Persistence)

PowerShell screen capture staged for Tor exfiltration - CryptoBandits clipper AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the CryptoBandits screenshot-exfiltration stage: PowerShell using GDI/Drawing screen-capture APIs (CopyFromScreen, Drawing.Bitmap, PrimaryScreen, BitBlt). Microsoft specifically flagged PowerShell-based screen capture as a behavioural indicator for this campaign. Rationale: Targets the article's screenshot-exfiltration capability via the specific .NET screen-capture API tokens Microsoft called out for PowerShell-based screen capture; these strings rarely appear in benign command lines. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html
ATT&CKT1113 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT remote-support / monitoring scripts that screenshot a user session for diagnostics
  • Screen-recording or kiosk-monitoring agents implemented in PowerShell
  • QA/test-automation harnesses capturing screenshots of the desktop
  • DLP or insider-risk tooling that periodically captures screen state
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","monitoringhost.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full PowerShell command line - confirm it builds a Bitmap from PrimaryScreen and where the image is saved/sent; check the parent (wscript/cscript points to CryptoBandits). 2) Contain: if malicious, isolate the host, kill the PowerShell + script-host tree, and block ugate.exe / the script hashes. 3) Hunt: correlate with ugate.exe execution and 127.0.0.1:9050 SOCKS activity on the same host to confirm screenshots are leaving via Tor; sweep the fleet for the same API token usage from a script-host parent.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("CopyFromScreen","Drawing.Bitmap","FromImage","PrimaryScreen","BitBlt")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("CopyFromScreen","Drawing.Bitmap","FromImage","PrimaryScreen","BitBlt")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PowerShell Screen Capture API Usage (CryptoBandits Exfiltration)

USB LNK worm cloning documents into shortcuts - CryptoBandits propagation AIDelivery Medium
Detects the CryptoBandits worm component cloning harvested DOC/XLSX/PDF files into same-named .lnk shortcuts: a script host (wscript/cscript) creating multiple .lnk files in a short span. The original documents are hidden so the user clicks the malicious shortcut instead. Rationale: Encodes the article's propagation mechanic - the worm scans the USB drive for DOC/XLSX/PDF, hides them, and creates same-named .lnk files pointing to the worm; a script-host creating 3+ shortcuts at once is a tight behavioural signature of that cloning loop. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://cyberinsider.com/microsoft-warns-of-usb-worm-like-malware-using-tor-for-stealth/
ATT&CKT1091 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Logon or deployment VBScripts that drop multiple Start Menu / Desktop shortcuts during app install
  • User profile setup scripts that recreate pinned shortcuts at first sign-in
  • Backup/sync tooling wrapped in a script host that rebuilds .lnk references
  • Software packaging tools generating shortcut sets via cscript
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install", "setup", "deploy", @"\Start Menu\") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the created .lnk targets - CryptoBandits shortcuts point back to wscript/cscript running the worm script and their names mirror real DOC/XLSX/PDF files now hidden in the same folder. Check the folder for hidden originals. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the script-host tree, quarantine the worm script and .lnk files, and scan/eject any connected removable media. 3) Hunt: enumerate other drives/hosts that mounted the same USB, and look for the paired scheduled-task persistence and ugate.exe execution to confirm full infection.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize LnkCount = dcount(FileName), LnkFiles = make_set(FileName, 20),
            Folders = make_set(FolderPath, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where LnkCount >= 3
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".lnk"
| summarize LnkCount = dcount(TargetFileName), Files = make_set(TargetFileName, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where LnkCount >= 3
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe) @TargetFilename:(*.lnk OR *.LNK)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i TargetFileName=/\.lnk$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=LnkCount))
| LnkCount >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Filesystem.file_name) as lnk_count values(Filesystem.file_name) as lnk_files min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" AND (Filesystem.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) AND Filesystem.action="created" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where lnk_count >= 3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Filesystem.file_name) as lnk_count values(Filesystem.file_name) as lnk_files min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" AND (Filesystem.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) AND Filesystem.action="created" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where lnk_count >= 3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

Internet-facing PraisonAI platform booting on default JWT secret (CVE-2026-47410) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts hosts running praisonai-platform's documented entry point bound to 0.0.0.0 (python -m praisonai_platform / uvicorn praisonai_platform.api.app). Because PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET/PLATFORM_ENV are set nowhere in the package, any such exposed instance signs session JWTs with the public literal 'dev-secret-change-me' and is pre-auth forgeable. Surfaces the vulnerable deployment so an analyst can confirm the env vars are actually set. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact documented entry point strings (praisonai_platform, uvicorn praisonai_platform.api.app, --host 0.0.0.0) — the article states neither PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET nor PLATFORM_ENV is set anywhere in the package, so any matching internet-bound process is the vulnerable default state. Cross-checked against GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 and the GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai-platform/CVE-2026-47410/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/praisonai-cve-2026-44338-auth-bypass.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/staging instance where PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET is exported in the shell or systemd unit (not visible on cmdline) so the deployment is actually safe
  • Container CI smoke-test that boots the server transiently then tears down
  • Reverse-proxy fronted deployment where 0.0.0.0 binding is intentional and the secret is set via Docker secret/env-file
  • Security team running the package in a lab to reproduce the advisory
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: On the surfaced host, check the running process environment for PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET (e.g. `cat /proc/<pid>/environ | tr '\0' '\n' | grep PLATFORM_`) — if absent or equal to 'dev-secret-change-me', the instance is forgeable. 2) CONTAIN: Pull the service off the public interface (firewall the port / bind to localhost), export a strong random PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET and PLATFORM_ENV=production, restart, and invalidate all outstanding sessions (every issued JWT was signed with the public key). 3) HUNT: Review the web/proxy logs for this service for the workspace-member enumeration and owner-gated DELETE activity (see companion UCs) to determine if forgery was already exercised.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "praisonai_platform"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("uvicorn", "-m praisonai_platform", "praisonai_platform.api.app")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai_platform"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("uvicorn", "-m praisonai_platform", "praisonai_platform.api.app")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI workspace/member destruction via owner-gated routes (forged-JWT takeover impact) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects successful DELETE requests against praisonai-platform's owner-gated routes — DELETE /workspaces/{workspace_id} (full workspace + contained resources) and DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id} (legitimate-member eviction). With the auth bypass these are reachable by an attacker holding only a forged owner JWT, yielding irrecoverable lock-out (A:H). Rationale: Pivots on the advisory's exact owner-gated route names (DELETE /workspaces/{workspace_id} and DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id}) called out as the resource-destruction / lock-out endpoints. Web-tier only because forgery and verification happen in-process with no endpoint signal. Cross-checked against the GitHub and GitLab advisories. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai-platform/CVE-2026-47410/
ATT&CKT1485 T1531 T1606
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine workspace owner deleting a workspace they no longer need
  • Admin offboarding a departed employee via DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id}
  • Automated cleanup job pruning stale demo/trial workspaces
  • QA teardown of test workspaces in a non-prod tenant
Suppression filter
| where CIp !in ("<known-admin-egress-ips>")  // remove this line and substitute your real admin egress CIDRs via an ip range watchlist; alternatively join to an allowlist of legitimate owner UPNs on CsUsername
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the source IP, User-Agent and any captured CsUsername for the DELETE; correlate the same source against the member-enumeration UC and the host-exposure UC — a delete preceded by a GET /{workspace_id}/members burst from the same IP strongly indicates forged-token takeover rather than a real owner. 2) CONTAIN: If forgery is suspected, rotate PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET immediately (this invalidates every forged and legitimate token), block the source IP at the proxy/WAF, and restore the deleted workspace/members from backup. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all DELETE and owner-gated mutation calls (member role changes, resource deletes) from the same IP/UA across every workspace to scope the blast radius.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsMethod == "DELETE"
| where CsUriStem matches regex @"(?i)^/workspaces/[^/]+/?$"
     or CsUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/[^/]+/members/[^/]+/?$"
| where ScStatus between (200 .. 299)
| project TimeGenerated, CIp, CsUsername, CsHost, CsMethod, CsUriStem, ScStatus, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI workspace member enumeration harvesting owner user_ids (pre-takeover recon) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a single source listing members across many workspaces via GET /{workspace_id}/members. The advisory states the response (List[MemberResponse], each carrying user_id and role) is how an attacker learns a workspace owner's uuid4 id — the one extra fact needed to forge an owner token and pivot from anonymous bypass to targeted owner takeover. Rationale: Pivots on the advisory's named recon primitive: GET /{workspace_id}/members returns each member's user_id and role to any member, which is exactly how an attacker obtains an owner's otherwise-unguessable uuid4 id. Fan-out across many workspaces from one source is the high-fidelity discriminator versus a real owner viewing their own one workspace. Threshold-based so no Sigma. Cross-checked against GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai-platform/CVE-2026-47410/
ATT&CKT1087 T1606
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/support console legitimately iterating member lists across many workspaces
  • Billing or analytics service account that periodically reads membership for all workspaces
  • Internal vulnerability scanner crawling the API surface
  • A power user who genuinely owns/belongs to many workspaces and opens each members page in a session
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "PraisonAI-Admin" and CsUsername !in ("svc-billing", "svc-analytics")  // suppress known internal service accounts/tools that legitimately sweep member lists
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the source IP/UA and whether it maps to a known service account or admin tool; an unfamiliar IP reading 5+ workspaces' member lists in minutes is the harvesting signal. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source at the proxy/WAF and, if the host-exposure UC confirms the instance runs on the default secret, rotate PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET and set PLATFORM_ENV=production to kill the forgery primitive before owner-id harvesting can be weaponised. 3) HUNT: Pivot the same source forward in time to any owner-gated mutation (DELETE workspace/member, role change) — see the destruction UC — to confirm whether harvested ids were used to forge owner tokens.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CsMethod == "GET"
| where CsUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/[^/]+/members/?$"
| where ScStatus between (200 .. 299)
| summarize WorkspacesEnumerated = dcount(CsUriStem), SampleRoutes = make_set(CsUriStem, 10), TotalReqs = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CIp, CsUsername, UserAgent, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where WorkspacesEnumerated >= 5   // one source reading the member list of 5+ distinct workspaces in 10 min = owner-id harvesting, not normal owner browsing
| order by WorkspacesEnumerated desc
APPLICATION

PraisonAI multiedit arbitrary write to SSH/shell/cloud-cred files by python process AIInstallation High
Hunts a PraisonAI agent (python) abusing the unvalidated `multiedit` filepath parameter to overwrite security-sensitive files outside the workspace — ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.bashrc/.profile, ~/.aws/credentials, .env. This is the write primitive of GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 used for persistence/privilege escalation, and is article-specific because it ties the named tool's host process to writes against the exact protected paths the advisory calls out. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact write-target paths (~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.bashrc, ~/.aws/credentials, .env) bound to the python host process of the named multiedit tool; high-fidelity because authorized_keys/.bashrc writes by an interpreter are rare. Cross-checked against the GitHub Advisory and the broader PraisonAI path-traversal advisory cluster. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/praisonai/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4171215/praisonai-vulnerability-gets-scanned-within-4-hours-of-disclosure.html
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1546.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Python application/deployment script writing its own project-local .env file inside the app workspace
  • Configuration-management tooling written in Python (Ansible local modules, custom provisioning) updating ~/.bashrc or ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
  • Developer Jupyter/python session legitimately editing dotfiles during environment setup
  • Cloud SDK helper writing ~/.aws/credentials during an authorized `aws configure`-style automation
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ ".env" and FolderPath has_any ("/site-packages/","/node_modules/","/.venv/","/venv/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent chain — confirm the writer is a PraisonAI agent/CLI (look for 'praisonai'/'multiedit') and whether the target path is outside the agent's intended workspace. Capture the before/after file contents (esp. authorized_keys new keys, .bashrc appended commands). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the agent process, revoke/rotate any keys or cloud credentials in the touched files, and remove attacker-added authorized_keys entries. 3) Hunt: pin praisonai version (must be >= 4.6.61); search the same host and peer agents for multiedit reads of secrets (see credential-read UC), unexpected outbound C2 from python, and downstream use of stolen ~/.aws/credentials in cloud logs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "python" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","multiedit")
| where (FileName =~ "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh/")
     or FileName in~ (".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc",".bash_aliases")
     or (FileName =~ "credentials" and FolderPath has "/.aws/")
     or FileName =~ ".env"
     or (FileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","authorized_keys") and FolderPath has "/.ssh/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has "python" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","multiedit")
| where (TargetFileName =~ "authorized_keys" and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh/")
     or TargetFileName in~ (".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc")
     or (TargetFileName =~ "credentials" and TargetFilePath has "/.aws/")
     or TargetFileName =~ ".env"
     or (TargetFileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519") and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI multiedit secret-file read (/etc/shadow, id_rsa, .aws/credentials, .env) by python AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the read/exfil primitive of GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47: a python-hosted PraisonAI agent opening sensitive secret files via the unvalidated multiedit filepath (incl. dry_run diff leakage). Targets the exact files the advisory names — /etc/shadow, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials, .env. Requires open/read telemetry (auditd watches or CrowdStrike FileOpenInfo) since Defender DeviceFileEvents does not emit read-only access. Rationale: Targets the precise secret paths the advisory cites as readable via the unvalidated multiedit tool, scoped to the python interpreter that hosts PraisonAI; defender_kql intentionally left empty because Defender DeviceFileEvents does not record read-only opens, so the detection leans on auditd/FileOpenInfo. Validated against the GHSA write-up and the PraisonAI advisory cluster. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/praisonai/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1003.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Python automation reading its own project .env at startup (inside workspace)
  • Python-based config tooling reading ~/.aws/credentials during an authorized cloud operation
  • Backup/inventory agents written in Python touching /etc/shadow on a hardened host
  • Security scanners or compliance scripts (python) auditing shadow/SSH key permissions
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reader is PraisonAI (command line / parent contains praisonai|multiedit) and that the file is outside any legitimate workspace; check whether dry_run diff output of these files was returned to a chat/agent transcript. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop the agent, and immediately rotate exposed secrets — SSH private keys, AWS access keys, anything in the read .env; force-expire AWS sessions. 3) Hunt: correlate the read timestamp with outbound python network connections (possible exfil) and with subsequent use of the leaked AWS keys in CloudTrail from new source IPs; check peer hosts running the same vulnerable PraisonAI build.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "type=PATH" or SyslogMessage has "type=SYSCALL" or ProcessName in ("audisp-syslog","auditd")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/shadow","/.ssh/id_rsa","/.ssh/id_ed25519","/.aws/credentials",".env")
| where SyslogMessage has "python"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI install/upgrade activity (verify version >= 4.6.61) AIWeaponization Low
Surfaces hosts where the vulnerable PraisonAI package (pip:praisonai < 4.6.61, fixed for GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) is being installed or upgraded, so exposure can be confirmed and patched. Exposure/hardening hunt rather than active-attack detection; pair with endpoint software inventory to confirm the resolved version. Rationale: Uses the advisory's concrete fixed-version boundary (praisonai 4.6.61) and package name to flag install/upgrade events for exposure triage; confidence is Low because it catches install commands (not container-baked images) and does not by itself prove the resolved version — confirm via software inventory/TVM. Cross-referenced with the GitHub Advisory fixed-version metadata. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/praisonai/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • CI/CD build agents reinstalling dependencies including praisonai during normal pipeline runs
  • Developer creating a fresh virtualenv and pip-installing the project's requirements
  • Container image bake steps shown as process events on build hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: from the command line determine the requested version; then query endpoint software inventory / `pip show praisonai` on the host to get the actually-installed version and compare to 4.6.61. 2) Contain: if < 4.6.61, prioritize upgrade to >= 4.6.61; on internet-exposed or chatbot deployments using auto_approve_tools=True, restrict the multiedit tool or gate it behind approval until patched. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts/containers running praisonai (inventory + this query org-wide), then run the multiedit read/write UCs against those hosts to check for actual exploitation before the patch landed.

| where ProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","upgrade","-U"," add ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Node.js MCP server reachable from public clients (unauthenticated MCPServer exposure) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] GHSA-j4f3-55x4-r6q2: npm PraisonAI MCPServer exposes unauthent
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PraisonAI MCP server (node) spawns shell/LOLBin child after external connection · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Node.js MCP server reachable from public clients (unauthenticated MCPServer exposure) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core PraisonAI MCPServer flaw: startHttp() calls listen(port) with no host arg, binding to the unspecified address (observed '::') so the HTTP JSON-RPC transport is reachable on all interfaces. This surfaces Node listeners accepting inbound connections from public source IPs — the precondition for unauthenticated tools/call. Rationale: Targets the article's root cause — httpServer.listen(port) with no host binds to '::' (the PoV's observed bindAddress), making the MCP HTTP transport reachable off-host. Inbound-accept on node from a Public RemoteIP is the exposure that unauthenticated tools/call depends on. Cross-checked against GHSA-4qq2-2j2x-x62c and the Network-AI GHSA-fj4g-2p96-q6m3 (same '0.0.0.0 + no auth' MCP pattern) plus Censys-reported mass MCP exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/praisonai/GHSA-4qq2-2j2x-x62c/ • https://github.com/Jovancoding/Network-AI/security/advisories/GHSA-fj4g-2p96-q6m3 • https://www.anvilogic.com/threat-reports/mcp-server-auth-flaws
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internet-facing Node app (Express/Next.js) intentionally bound to 0.0.0.0 on the host
  • Public load-balancer / uptime-monitor health probes hitting the Node port
  • Dev server bound to all interfaces in a DMZ or cloud VM with a public IP
  • Reverse-proxy host where the Node origin legitimately serves external clients
  • Container/k8s node with NodePort service exposing the app publicly by design
Suppression filter
| where LocalPort !in (80, 443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the LocalPort and process — confirm whether it is the PraisonAI MCPServer (check the app's startup code for server.start({port}) / node_modules/praisonai) versus a sanctioned web app. Pull the RemoteIPs and check for non-business geographies/ASNs. 2) Contain: if it is an MCP server, restrict the listener to 127.0.0.1 (or firewall the port to trusted CIDRs) and front it with an authenticating reverse proxy; block the offending source IPs at the edge. 3) Hunt: pivot the same DeviceId into UC2 (child-process spawns by that node PID) and UC3 (tools/call request bodies) to determine whether tools were actually invoked.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 50) by DeviceName, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc

PraisonAI MCP server (node) spawns shell/LOLBin child after external connection AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts post-exploitation of the unauthenticated tools/call dispatcher: registered MCP tools commonly wrap code execution and run with the server process privileges. This correlates a Node listener accepting an inbound public connection with that same node PID spawning a command interpreter/LOLBin within 5 minutes — i.e. an unauthenticated caller driving server-side tool execution. Rationale: Maps the article's Impact section — tool handlers 'run with the server process privileges' and an unauthenticated caller can 'drive the same actions' including 'code execution.' The Defender variant ties the inbound public reach (server PID owning the socket) to a child spawn by the same PID, turning a noisy node→shell pattern into a high-fidelity unauth-RCE signal. Corroborated by GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj (unauthenticated workflow execution) and PraisonAI unauth-RCE via tool_override.py. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai/CVE-2026-44334/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / native module builds spawning cmd.exe during npm install
  • electron-builder or packaging tooling shelling out to powershell/cmd
  • CI/build agents running Node test runners that invoke shell scripts
  • pm2/forever/nodemon process managers spawning shells
  • Legitimately-registered MCP tools that are designed to run shell commands
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("node-gyp","electron-builder","npm-cli.js","node_modules\\.bin","prebuild-install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and the correlated RemoteIP/LocalPort — distinguish a build-tool shell (node-gyp/npm) from attacker commands (recon, download, encoded payloads). Confirm the parent node process is an MCP server. 2) Contain: kill the node MCP process, isolate the host, and rotate any server-side credentials/API keys the MCP tools had access to (they ran under the server identity). 3) Hunt: enumerate all tools/resources the server registered, review UC3 for the tools/call bodies that triggered execution, and sweep other hosts running the praisonai package for the same node→shell pattern.
let Window = 5m;
let InboundReach = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | project ConnTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, ServerPid=InitiatingProcessId, RemoteIP, LocalPort;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| join kind=inner InboundReach on DeviceId
| where InitiatingProcessId == ServerPid
| where Timestamp between (ConnTime .. ConnTime + Window)
| project ConnTime, SpawnTime=Timestamp, DelaySec=datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ConnTime), DeviceName, AccountName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by ConnTime desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\curl.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PraisonAI AgentOS Node server exposed to non-loopback on default port 8000
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Vulnerable PraisonAI npm package present (dist/os/agentos.js) on managed hosts
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Unauthenticated PraisonAI AgentOS API hits: GET /api/agents enumeration + POST /api/chat invocation · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
PraisonAI AgentOS Node server exposed to non-loopback on default port 8000 AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for a node.exe process accepting inbound network connections from non-loopback/public source addresses on TCP 8000, the configuration the advisory describes when AgentOS keeps its default host '0.0.0.0' and is started with serve({ port: 8000 }). This surfaces PraisonAI AgentOS instances that are network-reachable without authentication. Rationale: Anchors on the advisory's named defaults: AgentOS binds host '0.0.0.0' with no auth and the PoV/serve example listens on port 8000 via a node process. Inbound acceptance from a non-loopback source on node:8000 is the network signature of an internet/LAN-reachable unauthenticated AgentOS. Port is configurable so this is hunting-tier; cross-checked against the sibling Python AgentOS advisory and Sysdig's observation of internet-wide scanning of these instances. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892R-P3JQ-JP24 • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal Node/Express dev servers (webpack-dev-server, http-server, json-server) that also default to port 8000
  • Authorized internal access to a PraisonAI AgentOS instance that has been correctly fronted by auth/reverse proxy
  • Vulnerability scanners / Nessus / internal pentest sweeps probing 8000 across the estate
  • Containerized microservices that legitimately publish 8000 to the host network
  • Health-check or load-balancer probes to the listener from internal monitoring subnets
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "agentos", "AgentOS") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "praisonai"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the listening process is PraisonAI by inspecting InitiatingProcessCommandLine / the node working directory for a node_modules/praisonai path, and identify whether SampleSources are internal or public. 2) Contain: if reachable from untrusted networks, firewall TCP 8000 to loopback/management only and restart AgentOS bound to 127.0.0.1, or place an authenticating reverse proxy in front. 3) Hunt: pull web/proxy logs for the same host to see whether /api/agents or /api/chat were actually hit (UC2), and review agent tool/credential scope for signs of abuse.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8000
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where RemoteIPType != "Loopback" and RemoteIP != "127.0.0.1" and RemoteIP != "::1"
| summarize Connections = count(), DistinctSources = dcount(RemoteIP), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleSources = make_set(RemoteIP, 20) by DeviceName, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
ImNetworkSession

| where DstPortNumber == 8000
| where NetworkDirection =~ "Inbound"

| order by LastSeen desc

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 LocalPort=8000 ContextImageFileName=/node\.exe$/i

Unauthenticated PraisonAI AgentOS API hits: GET /api/agents enumeration + POST /api/chat invocation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects HTTP access to the AgentOS routes /api/agents (discloses agent names, roles and instruction prefixes) and /api/chat (invokes the agent without credentials) returning 200. Same source IP touching both endpoints, or the documented scanner User-Agent, indicates the read-then-invoke exploitation flow the advisory describes. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact route literals (apiPrefix default '/api' → /api/agents, /api/chat) and the 200-status fail-open behaviour (patched servers return 401). Requiring the same client to hit BOTH the enumeration and invocation routes encodes the read-then-invoke flow; the CVE-Detector/1.0 UA is the real scanner string Sysdig observed probing the identical endpoints on the sibling CVE-2026-44338. Defender XDR has no inbound-HTTP-request table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; FDR/Datadog likewise don't ship web access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892R-P3JQ-JP24 • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/praisonai-cve-2026-44338-auth-bypass.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers or QA exercising /api/agents and /api/chat from a browser/Postman during testing
  • Application uptime monitors or synthetic transactions hitting both routes on a schedule
  • A correctly authenticated front-end legitimately calling both endpoints from one egress IP
  • Internal load testing tools generating GET+POST traffic to the AgentOS API
  • Security scanners other than CVE-Detector cataloguing the endpoints during an authorized assessment
Suppression filter
| where CIp !startswith "10." and CIp !startswith "192.168." and not (ipv4_is_in_range(CIp, "172.16.0.0/12"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether CIp is external/untrusted and whether the requests carried an Authorization header (check WAF/proxy header logs if available); a 200 on /api/chat from an external IP with no auth = confirmed unauthenticated invocation. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the proxy/WAF, take the AgentOS instance off untrusted networks, and rotate any credentials/tokens reachable by the invoked agent (env vars, downstream API keys). 3) Hunt: review the agent's tool/MCP/business-action logs for actions triggered in the request window, and pivot to UC1 to enumerate every exposed AgentOS listener in the estate.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsUriStem in~ ("/api/agents", "/api/chat")
| where ScStatus == 200
| summarize Requests = count(), Methods = make_set(CsMethod), Endpoints = make_set(CsUriStem), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CIp, CsHost
| extend Scanner = iff(UserAgents has "CVE-Detector/1.0", "yes", "no")
| where (set_has_element(Endpoints, "/api/agents") and set_has_element(Endpoints, "/api/chat")) or Scanner == "yes"
| order by LastSeen desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI npm package present (dist/os/agentos.js) on managed hosts AIInstallation High
Asset-exposure hunt for the affected component: the file dist/os/agentos.js dropped under a node_modules/praisonai path (shipped in npm praisonai >=1.6.0,<=1.7.1), or an 'npm install praisonai' command. Identifies which hosts actually carry the unauthenticated AgentOS code so they can be hardened before exploitation. Rationale: Deterministic article artifact: the advisory names the affected component path src/praisonai-ts/.../os/agentos.ts which ships as dist/os/agentos.js inside the npm praisonai tarball (boundary: <=1.5.4 did not ship dist/os). Matching agentos.js under a praisonai folder pins the exact vulnerable code on disk with near-zero ambiguity. Affected range >=1.6.0,<=1.7.1 confirmed in the advisory; the unauthenticated-by-default behaviour corroborated by the sibling AgentOS advisory GHSA-892R-P3JQ-JP24. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892R-P3JQ-JP24 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate, authorized PraisonAI deployment by an internal AI/ML team
  • CI/CD build agents that npm-install praisonai during pipeline runs
  • Developer workstations with the package in a local project's node_modules
  • Container image builds layering the package (file write seen at build time)
  • Security team intentionally staging the package for testing/reproduction
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installed version (read package.json under the praisonai folder, or the InitiatingProcessCommandLine for an 'npm install praisonai@x'); flag any version in >=1.6.0,<=1.7.1. 2) Contain: ensure the AgentOS server is not started with the default host (bind 127.0.0.1), require an auth token, and firewall the listener; no fixed npm version existed at advisory time, so treat all installs as needing compensating controls. 3) Hunt: for each affected host, pivot to UC1 (is it listening on a non-loopback interface?) and UC2 (has anyone hit /api/agents or /api/chat?) to distinguish merely-installed from actively-exposed-and-probed.

| where FileName =~ "agentos.js"
| where FolderPath has "praisonai" and FolderPath has @"\dist\os\"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Paths = make_set(FolderPath, 10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
